design_detail: Open-label randomized two-period crossover trial in 13 healthy Japanese men with fully active aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2*1/*1): the same amount of sake drunk with or without added mineral water taken in between, in two sessions, with standard meals, an overnight stay and repeated measures of breath ethanol and acetaldehyde, a one-minute Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) and six visual analogue symptom ratings from before drinking to the next day (schedule in the exposure field). Registered UMIN000050305. Funded by the sake brewer that made the test drink.
can_establish: Whether, in a small group of healthy men drinking a fixed amount of sake under controlled conditions, adding a large volume of water during drinking changes breath alcohol and acetaldehyde or the next-morning symptom ratings and DSST performance by a large amount.
cannot_establish: Whether water during drinking makes a small or moderate difference to hangover (13 participants; no intervals reported); whether it helps in real life, where water may reduce how much and how fast people drink (alcohol was fixed here); whether results apply to women, to people with the less active ALDH2 variant or other genetic backgrounds, to other drinks, or to smaller amounts of water; and whether people actually had a hangover (no hangover scale was used).

sample.recruitment: Not described beyond healthy Japanese men studied at the Oita University Hospital Clinical Trial Unit, January to March 2023.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: men aged 20 to 50, body mass index 18.0 to 30.0, ALDH2*1/*1 genotype (checked by PCR on cheek cells), a history of drinking more than 100 g of pure alcohol per day (as printed), and no significant health problems. Excluded: history of alcohol abuse or alcohol allergy, regular medication, liver disease, or abnormal findings at clinical examination.
sample.demographics: Mean age 36.2 years (SD 9.6), height 172.5 cm (6.0), weight 71.5 kg (8.2), body mass index 24.0 (2.0); all men, all Japanese.
sample.attrition: Of 16 who consented, 2 withdrew and 14 took part; one was excluded because severe abdominal fullness stopped him finishing the water, leaving 13 in a per-protocol analysis. When the withdrawals occurred, and the excluded man's data, are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Men only; only the fully active ALDH2 genotype, which the authors say excludes the roughly 40% of East Asians with the less active variant; people able to drink at least 100 g of alcohol in a day; a per-protocol analysis that dropped the one participant who could not tolerate the water condition.

exposure.measurement: Supervised drinking in the clinical trial unit, with the amounts of sake and water fixed by body weight and drunk at an even pace over one hour.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: Japanese sake (15% alcohol by volume) equal to 1.3 g/kg pure alcohol, drunk over one hour from 9 p.m., alone or with 15 mL/kg mineral water taken in between drinks; mean sake 749 mL (range 598 to 967) and mean water 1,072 mL (855 to 1,383). Total fluid in the water condition about 1,800 mL in the hour. About 6 hours of sleep, waking 7 hours after drinking ended. Sessions at least one week apart. Measures before drinking, immediately and one hour after drinking ended, and at several times from 7 to 15 hours after; the next-morning DSST differences discussed are at 7 and 8 hours. A standard dinner at least 2 hours before drinking and a standard breakfast 10 hours after; one 550 mL bottle of water allowed overnight and another from breakfast, in both conditions.
exposure.polysubstance: Regular medication excluded; other drugs and smoking not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Next-morning measures began 7 hours after drinking ended; breath ethanol at that point is shown only in a figure.

comparison.controls: The same men drinking the same amount of sake without the added water, in the other period.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover with a washout between sessions (interval in the exposure field); order randomized, method not described; the number of men in each sequence is not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not relevant to the within-person comparison. Sleep was not measured, and expectations about water were not recorded.

outcomes.instruments: Breath ethanol and acetaldehyde by sensor gas chromatography (detection limits 0.2 ppm and 5 ppb); DSST, number of correct symbol matches in one minute, analysed as change from the pre-drinking score; 100 mm visual analogue scales for facial flushing, headache, nausea, concentration, sleepiness and feeling exhilarated; all before drinking, shortly after drinking and at several times the next morning (schedule in the exposure field).
outcomes.validity_norms: The DSST is a standard processing-speed test; the six visual analogue items are not a validated hangover scale, and no hangover severity questionnaire was used.
outcomes.operationalization: Hangover was inferred by the authors from higher headache and nausea ratings and lower concentration ratings early the next morning; a difference between conditions at any time point was the test of effect.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, by design (exploratory study), across nine outcomes, each tested at several time points.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: open label. Symptoms were self-rated by participants who knew which condition they were in.

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported numerically. Means, SDs and differences appear only in figures (images; values not extracted). Text: no significant difference in breath ethanol or acetaldehyde at any time, with acetaldehyde point estimates slightly higher with water shortly after drinking; DSST change from baseline lower with water immediately after drinking (p = 0.01) and higher with water at the first two next-morning tests (p = 0.05 and 0.08, described as not significant); no significant difference in any of the six symptom ratings. The publisher's figure descriptions, which it says were written with AI support, describe the without-water curves as peaking higher in the headache, sleepiness and exhilaration panels; these were not used as data.
analysis.covariates: Linear mixed-effects model with drink condition and period as fixed effects and participant as a random effect; whether a separate model was fitted at each time point is not stated.
analysis.preregistration_detail: UMIN-CTR 000050305, registered before the trial according to the paper. The registry record was not read, so the registered primary outcome and target sample (the paper gives a target of 20 and a minimum of 6) could not be compared with the report.
analysis.selective_reporting: No numerical results for any outcome are given in text or tables; only the DSST has p-values. The target of 20 participants was not reached and no reason is given.
analysis.power: Exploratory; no formal calculation in advance. The authors state afterwards that with 13 participants power was barely 0.8 to detect an effect size of 1 at a one-sided 5% level, so smaller effects could be missed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 13 men, adding a large amount of water while drinking sake did not detectably change breath ethanol or acetaldehyde, or any of six next-morning symptom ratings, compared with the same sake without water; DSST performance was worse with water right after drinking (when several participants reported bloating) and, without reaching significance, slightly better with water the next morning. No numerical estimates or intervals are reported, so the size of any effect that was missed cannot be bounded.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title states that water intake during drinking "does not alleviate hangover symptoms", and the abstract concludes it did not affect hangover. Gaps: (1) a non-significant result in 13 people, with power only for a very large effect, is read as absence of effect; (2) no hangover scale was used, and the hangover state is inferred from figure trends; (3) the conclusion speculates that water helps in daily life by limiting how much people drink, which the fixed-dose design could not test, and also suggests water may slightly improve next-morning performance from a p of 0.05 to 0.08 the authors call non-significant; (4) the funding statement says the funder had no role in analysis, while two of the four authors employed by the funder did the formal analysis. The Discussion does list the small sample, men only, open label, one genotype and one drink as limits.

timeline.event: Mackus et al. (Alcohol, 2024) on drinking water to prevent or relieve hangover, cited by the authors as agreeing; not read here and not in the library's references.
This trial: by the authors' account the first randomized crossover study of water during drinking with alcohol, water and food controlled.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small, open-label, industry-funded crossover trial. It is the only randomized test of water during drinking that the authors knew of; the earlier work they cite on water and hangover was not randomized.

funding.funder: Sanwa Shurui Corporation, a sake brewer, which made the test drink (Waka Botan sake); the statement says the funder was not involved in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to publish.
funding.declared_conflicts: Four authors (SK, AN, KM, MK) were employed by the Research Laboratory of Sanwa Shurui Co., Ltd.; the others declare no conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: Per the author-contribution statement, two of the employees (SK and MK) did the formal analysis and data curation and all four contributed to conceptualization or methods, which sits uneasily with the statement that the funder had no role in design or analysis.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized crossover trial, preregistered with a validated hangover severity scale as the primary outcome, in women and men of different genetic backgrounds, comparing water with no water at amounts people actually drink, with the alcohol fixed in one comparison and free (self-chosen) in another so that any effect through drinking less can be seen, and with sleep measured and outcomes rated blind where possible.

domains.note: Random assignment to sequence is stated, but how the sequence was generated and concealed is not, nor how many men were in each sequence.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: The washout between sessions (interval in the exposure field) is ample for a single evening of alcohol; period was in the model.
Open label. One man could not finish the water because of abdominal fullness and was dropped (per-protocol analysis); several others reported bloating during the water condition.
One of 14 participants excluded for a reason tied to the intervention, and his data are not reported; the two earlier withdrawals are not explained.

Symptoms were self-rated by participants who knew whether they had drunk water, a remedy the authors call widely believed to work. The breath measures are objective and the DSST less exposed. The expected direction of this bias favours water, so it does not explain the null result.
Registered, but the registered primary outcome could not be checked here; results are reported only as figures and p-values, at many time points without correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Overall high because the symptom outcomes were self-rated without blinding; other domains raise some concerns (randomization not described, per-protocol exclusion tied to the intervention, no numerical results). For the question this card is cited for, whether water during drinking reduced next-morning symptoms, the unblinded rating would be expected to favour water, so the null finding is not likely to be an artefact of it; its main weakness is imprecision. The trial may be cited as finding no detectable effect in 13 men at one fixed amount of sake, and not as showing that water has no effect.

key_findings.finding: Breath ethanol and acetaldehyde did not differ significantly between the water and no-water conditions at any time after drinking; acetaldehyde point estimates were slightly higher with water shortly after drinking, and the curves were almost identical by the next morning.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: DSST change from the pre-drinking score was lower with water immediately after drinking ended (p = 0.01) and higher with water at the first two next-morning tests (p = 0.05 and 0.08), which the authors call not statistically significant; scores then returned to pre-drinking levels in both conditions.
key_findings.note: No means, SDs or intervals are given in text; the 5% two-sided threshold was stated in advance, so p = 0.05 is on the boundary.

key_findings.finding: None of the six visual analogue ratings (facial flushing, headache, nausea, concentration, sleepiness, feeling exhilarated) differed significantly between conditions at any time point.

The authors read higher headache and nausea ratings and lower concentration ratings early the next morning as a hangover state, and higher flushing and mood ratings right after drinking as intoxication; these trends are shown only in figures.

Total fluid intake in the water condition was very large (amounts in the exposure field); several men reported abdominal bloating, and one dropped out with severe fullness; the authors suggest the bloating may explain the lower DSST score right after drinking.

The authors state that 13 participants gave power barely 0.8 to detect an effect size of 1 (one-sided 5% level), so smaller effects may have been missed; and that the design cannot separate drinking water between drinks from drinking the same alcohol diluted to about half strength.
Funding came from the sake brewer that made the test drink, and four of eight authors were employed by its research laboratory.
key_findings.locator: Funding Statement; Conflict of interests; Author contributions

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract state that water does not alleviate hangover symptoms, a conclusion of absence drawn from non-significant differences in 13 men, with no estimates or intervals reported and power only for an effect size of 1.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Title; Abstract › Conclusion; Discussions, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must say the evidence is insufficient to rule out a modest effect, not that water does not work.

reporting_issues.issue: The funding statement says the funder had no role in design, analysis or interpretation, but four authors were employed by the funder and two of them did the formal analysis and data curation (author contributions).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Funding Statement; Conflict of interests; Author contributions
reporting_issues.consequence: The funder's involvement is larger than the funding statement says; a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount the null result, which runs against a commercial interest in neither direction obviously.

reporting_issues.issue: The model is described differently in two places: the abstract names fixed effects for the test beverages and the number of administrations, the Methods name beverage and time (first and second periods), and how the difference at each time point was tested is not stated.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Methods; Methods › Statistical analyses
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysis cannot be reproduced from the text.

reporting_issues.issue: No numerical results (means, SDs, differences, intervals) are reported for any outcome; all values are in figures only. The data availability statement refers to online repositories whose names are said to be in the article, but none is named.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results; Figures 2 to 4; Data availability statement
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes cannot be computed, and the imprecision of the null result cannot be quantified.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusion suggests that water may slightly improve next-morning psychomotor function, from DSST differences with p = 0.05 and 0.08 that the Results call non-significant, and attributes the popular belief in water to drinking less, which the fixed-dose design did not test.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither statement is a finding of this trial.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the two conditions the Control group and the Water group, although every participant took part in both.
reporting_issues.consequence: Terminology only; the comparison is within-person.
